questions.problem: Find a vector that's tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{3}-1,{t}^{2}+1⟩$ at the point where $t=-2.$
questions.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=-2,$ the vector ${r}^{′}(-2)$ is tangent to the curve.

Let's calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=-2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2},2t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(-2) & =⟨3(-2)^{2},2(-2)⟩ \\  & =⟨12,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point where $t=-2$ is $⟨12,-4⟩.$

questions.problem: Find a tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=2\sqrt{3-t}\,i+(1-2t)\,j+(t+3)\,k$ at the point $P(2,-3,5).$
questions.worked_solution:
The point $P(2,-3,5)$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point, the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve.

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =2\,i-3\,j+5\,k \\ 2\sqrt{3-t}\,i+(1-2t)\,j+(t+3)\,k & =2\,i-3\,j+5\,k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3-t}=2 \\ 1-2t=-3 \\ t+3=5\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $t=2.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,-3,5)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(2).$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{3-t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+3)\,k \\  & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3-t}}\,i-2\,j+k \\ {r}^{′}(2) & =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3-2}}\,i-2\,j+k \\  & =-\,i-2\,j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point $P(2,-3,5)$ is $-\,i-2\,j+k.$

questions.problem: Find a tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=(3t+2)\,i+(6t+1)\,j+(1-4{t}^{2})\,k$ at the point $P(2,1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
The point $P(2,1,1)$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point, the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve.

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =2\,i+j+k \\ (3t+2)\,i+(6t+1)\,j+(1-4{t}^{2})\,k & =2\,i+j+k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}3t+2=2 \\ 6t+1=1 \\ 1-4{t}^{2}=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $t=0.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(2,1,1)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(0).$

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t+1)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-4{t}^{2})\,k \\  & =3\,i+6\,j-8t\,k \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =3\,i+6\,j-8(0)\,k \\  & =3\,i+6\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point $P(2,1,1)$ is $3\,i+6\,j.$

questions.problem: Find a tangent vector to the curve $r(t)=⟨{e}^{t},\,{e}^{-t},\,{t}^{2}⟩$ at the point where $t=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=0$,  the vector ${r}^{′}(0)$ is tangent to the curve.

Let's calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{e}^{t},\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{e}^{-t},\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,-{e}^{-t},\,2t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =⟨{e}^{0},\,-{e}^{-0},\,2\cdot 0⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point where $t=0$ is $⟨1,\,-1,\,0⟩.$

questions.problem: Find a vector that's tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨2(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,2(t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)⟩$ at the point where $t=\pi .$
questions.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=\pi $,  the vector ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ is tangent to the curve.

Let's calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[2(t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)],\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[2(t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)]⟩ \\  & =⟨2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,2(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\pi ) & =⟨2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ),\,2(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )⟩ \\  & =⟨2(1-(-1)),\,2(1+0)⟩ \\  & =⟨4,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at the point where $t=\pi $  is  $⟨4,\,2⟩$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Tangent Line to a Curve
questions.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}+1),1-5t⟩$ at the point where $t=0,$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
questions.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=0,$ the vector ${r}^{′}(0)$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as
 

$$
R(u)=r(0)+u{r}^{′}(0),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡({0}^{2}+1),1-5(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({t}^{2}+1)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-5t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2t}{{t}^{2}+1},-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0) & =⟨\frac{2(0)}{{0}^{2}+1},-5⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where $t=0$ is

$$
R(u)=⟨0,1⟩+u⟨0,-5⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=t\,i+({t}^{3}+1)\,j+{t}^{5}\,k$ at the point $P(1,2,1),$ 
valid for real values of $u?$
questions.worked_solution:
The point $P(1,2,1)$ is at the tip of $r(t)$ for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point,  the vector ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
R(u)=r({t}_{0})+u\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

 

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =i+2\,j+k \\ t\,i+({t}^{3}+1)\,j+{t}^{5}\,k & =i+2\,j+k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}t=1 \\ {t}^{3}+1=2 \\ {t}^{5}=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $t=1.$ This value also satifies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(1,2,1)$ is at the tip of the vector $r(1).$  

We calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+1)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{5})\,k \\  & =i+3{t}^{2}\,j+5{t}^{4}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(1) & =i+3(1)^{2}\,j+5(1)^{4}\,k \\  & =i+3\,j+5\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point $P(1,2,1)$ is 

$$
R(u)=i+2\,j+\,k+u(\,i+3\,j+5\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩$ at the point where $t=\pi ,$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
questions.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=\pi ,$ the vector ${r}^{′}(\pi )$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as
 

$$
R(u)=r(\pi )+u{r}^{′}(\pi ),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(\pi ):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\pi ) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=\pi :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\pi ) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ,-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ⟩ \\  & =⟨0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point where $t=\pi $ is

$$
R(u)=⟨-1,0⟩+u⟨0,1⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

questions.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=0,$ the vector ${r}^{′}(0)$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as
 

$$
R(u)=r(0)+u{r}^{′}(0),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t+5),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-{t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨3,-3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}

questions.problem: Which of the following gives the equation of the tangent to the curve $r(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+{sin}^{2}t\,k$ at the point corresponding to $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$  valid for all  real values of $u?$
questions.worked_solution:
At the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$,  the vector ${r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

 

$$
R(u)=r(\frac{\pi }{4})+u{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

 

First, we find $r(\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,j+{sin}^{2}(\frac{\pi }{4})\,k \\  & =\,i+\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({sin}^{2}t)\,k \\  & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${r}^{′}(t)$ at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,j-\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})k \\  & =\,i-\,j+\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the given curve at the point 
 where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
R(u)=\,i+\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k+u(\,i-\,j+\,k),\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Perpendicular to Another Vector
questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+1\,,\,2t-1⟩,$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨1\,,\,-2⟩.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1)\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t\,,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $⟨1\,,\,-2⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨1\,,\,-2⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨1\,,\,-2⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨1\,,\,-2⟩\cdot ⟨2t\,,\,2⟩ & =0 \\ 1\cdot 2t+(-2)\cdot 2 & =0 \\ 2t-4 & =0 \\ 2(t-2) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=2.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =⟨{(2)}^{2}+1\,,\,2(2)-1⟩=⟨5\,,\,3⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1\,,\,-2⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(5,3).$

questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+2t,4-{t}^{2}⟩,$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨0,-1⟩.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4-{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2t+2,-2t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $⟨0,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨0,-1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨0,-1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨0,-1⟩\cdot ⟨2t+2,-2t⟩ & =0 \\ 0(2t+2)+(-1)(-2t) & =0 \\ 2t & =0 \\ t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=0.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{0}^{2}+2(0),4-{0}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,4⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨0,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(0,4).$

questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}-1\,,\,{t}^{3}+1⟩,t\in (-\infty ,0)$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $⟨2\,,\,1⟩.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-1)\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t\,,\,3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $⟨2\,,\,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨2\,,\,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨2\,,\,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨2\,,\,1⟩\cdot ⟨2t\,,\,3{t}^{2}⟩ & =0 \\ 2\cdot 2t+1\cdot 3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ 4t+3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ t(4+3t) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $t\in (-\infty ,0)$, the only solution is $t=-\frac{4}{3}$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-\frac{4}{3}) & =⟨{(-\frac{4}{3})}^{2}-1\,,\,{(-\frac{4}{3})}^{3}+1⟩=⟨\frac{7}{9}\,,\,-\frac{37}{27}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $⟨2\,,\,-1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(\frac{7}{9}\,,\,-\frac{37}{27}).$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Perpendicular to Another Vector
questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=(t+2)\,i+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,j$, find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are perpendicular.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+2)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1})\,j \\  & =i+\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ [(t+2)\,i+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\,j]\cdot (i+\frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}}\,j) & =0 \\ (t+2)\cdot 1+\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}\cdot \frac{t}{\sqrt{{t}^{2}+1}} & =0 \\ t+2+t & =0 \\ 2t+2 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=-1.$ 

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1)=(-1+2)\,i+\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+1}\,j=i+\sqrt{2}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(1,\sqrt{2}).$

questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=t\,i+(1+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})\,j$, find all of the points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are perpendicular.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})\,j \\  & =i+t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ [t\,i+(1+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})\,j]\cdot (i+t\,j) & =0 \\ t\cdot 1+(1+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2})\cdot t & =0 \\ 2t+\frac{1}{2}{t}^{3} & =0 \\ t(4+{t}^{2}) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=0$ since $4+{t}^{2}>0$ for any $t.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0)=0\,i+(1+\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2})\,j=j,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(0,1).$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Parallel to Another Vector
questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{4}+4t\,,\,{t}^{3}-2t\,,\,2{t}^{3}-3t⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4}+4t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3}-3t)⟩ \\  & =⟨4{t}^{3}+4,\,3{t}^{2}-2,\,6{t}^{2}-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c\,⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c\,⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩ \\ ⟨4{t}^{3}+4,\,3{t}^{2}-2,\,6{t}^{2}-3⟩ & =c\,⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩ \\ ⟨4{t}^{3}+4,\,3{t}^{2}-2,\,6{t}^{2}-3⟩ & =⟨0\,,\,c\,,\,3c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}4{t}^{3}+4=0 \\ 3{t}^{2}-2=c \\ 6{t}^{2}-3=3c\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $t=-1.$ Substituting to the second equation, we get $c=1.$
These values also satisfy the third equation. 

Therefore, $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=-1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨(-1)^{4}+4(-1)\,,\,(-1)^{3}-2(-1)\,,\,2(-1)^{3}-3(-1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,\,1,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(-3,1,1).$

questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}-2t\,,\,{t}^{2}\,,\,8t-2{t}^{2}⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨1\,,\,2\,,\,0⟩.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8t-2{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨2t-2,\,2t,\,8-4t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c\,⟨1\,,\,2\,,\,0⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c\,⟨1\,,\,2\,,\,0⟩ \\ ⟨2t-2,\,2t,\,8-4t⟩ & =c\,⟨1\,,\,2\,,\,0⟩ \\ ⟨2t-2,\,2t,\,8-4t⟩ & =⟨c\,,\,2c\,,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2t-2=c \\ 2t=2c \\ 8-4t=0\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we obtain that $t=2.$ Substituting to the second equation, we get $c=2.$
These values also satisfy the first equation. 

Therefore, $⟨1\,,\,2\,,\,0⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=2.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2) & =⟨{2}^{2}-2(2)\,,\,{2}^{2}\,,\,8(2)-2(2)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,4,\,8⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1\,,\,2\,,\,0⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(0,4,8).$

questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{3}\,,\,{e}^{t}\,,\,{e}^{t-1}⟩$, find all points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t-1})⟩ \\  & =⟨3{t}^{2},\,{e}^{t},\,{e}^{t-1}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ ⟨{t}^{3}\,,\,{e}^{t}\,,\,{e}^{t-1}⟩ & =c\,⟨3{t}^{2},\,{e}^{t},\,{e}^{t-1}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

  

Equating the components gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{t}^{3}=c(3{t}^{2}) \\ {e}^{t}=c{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{t-1}=c{e}^{t-1}\end{aligned}
$$

From the second and third equations, we obtain that $c=1.$ Substituting $c=1$ into the first equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{3} & =3{t}^{2} \\ {t}^{3}-3{t}^{2} & =0 \\ {t}^{2}(t-3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the points corresponding to $t=0$, and $t=3.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{0}^{3},\,{e}^{0},\,{e}^{0-1}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,{e}^{-1}⟩ \\ r(3) & =⟨{3}^{3},\,{e}^{3},\,{e}^{3-1}⟩ \\  & =⟨27,\,{e}^{3},\,{e}^{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

 we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the points $(0,1,{e}^{-1})$ and $(27,{e}^{3},{e}^{2}).$

questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)={e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j$, find all points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$  

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{2t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j \\  & =2{e}^{2t}\,i+(2t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ {e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j & =c(2{e}^{2t}\,i+(2t+1)\,j) \\ {e}^{2t}\,i+({t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2})\,j & =2c{e}^{2t}\,i+c(2t+1)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $i$ and $j$ gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t}=2c{e}^{2t} \\ {t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2}=c(2t+1)\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain $c=\frac{1}{2}.$ Substituting $c=\frac{1}{2}$ into the second equality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}+t+\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}(2t+1) \\ {t}^{2} & =0 \\ t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel at the point corresponding to $t=0.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & ={e}^{0}\,i+({0}^{2}+0+\frac{1}{2})\,j \\  & =i+\frac{1}{2}\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(1,\frac{1}{2}).$

questions.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=t\,i+(2+{t}^{3})\,j+(1+{t}^{2})\,k$, find all points at which ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$   

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2+{t}^{3})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+{t}^{2})\,k \\  & =i+\,3{t}^{2}\,j+\,2t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $r(t)$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $r({t}_{0})=c\,{r}^{′}({t}_{0}).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =c\,{r}^{′}(t) \\ t\,i+(2+{t}^{3})\,j+(1+{t}^{2})\,k & =c(i+\,3{t}^{2}\,j+\,2t\,k).\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $i,j,$ and $k$ gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}t=c \\ 2+{t}^{3}=c(3{t}^{2}) \\ 1+{t}^{2}=c(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation we obtain $t=c.$ Substituting $c=t$ into the second equality gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}2+{t}^{3} & =3{t}^{3} \\ 2 & =2{t}^{3} \\ {t}^{3} & =1 \\ t & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This satisfies also the equation $1+{t}^{2}=c(2t).$
Therefore, $r$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =i+(2+{1}^{3})\,j+(1+{1}^{2})\,k \\  & =i+3\,j+2\,k,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $r(t)$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $P(1,3,2).$

canonical_examples.problem: Find a tangent vector to the curve $\mathbf r(t)=t\,\mathbf i+t^2\,\mathbf j+t^3\,\mathbf k$ at the point $P(1,1,1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The point $P(1,1,1)$ is at the tip of $\mathbf r(t)$ for some specific value $t_0$ of the parameter $t.$ At this point,  the vector $\mathbf r'(t_0)$ is tangent to the curve.

First, we find the value of $t$ that corresponds to $P.$ We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\,i+\,j+\,k \\ t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j+{t}^{3}\,k & =i+\,j+\,k,\end{aligned}
$$

and equating the coefficients of $\mathbf i, \mathbf j,$ and $\mathbf k$ yields the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}t=1 \\ {t}^{2}=1 \\ {t}^{3}=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $t=1.$ This value also satisfies the other two equations. Therefore, $P(1,1,1)$ is at the tip of the vector $\mathbf r(1).$  

Now, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=1\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})\,k \\  & =i+2t\,j+3{t}^{2}\,k \\ {r}^{′}(1) & =i+2(1)\,j+3(1)^{2}\,k \\  & =i+2\,j+3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to the given curve at at the point $P(1,1,1)$ is $\,\mathbf i+2\,\mathbf j+3\,\mathbf k.$

canonical_examples.problem: Find a parametrization of the tangent line to the curve $\mathbf r(t)=\left\langle \cos{t}, \: \sin{t},\: 4t^2\right\rangle$ at the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let  $P$ be the point at the tip of the vector $\mathbf r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right ).$  At this point,  the vector $\mathbf r'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right )$ is tangent to the curve, so the tangent line to the curve at $P$ can be parametrized as

$$
\mathbf R(u)=\mathbf r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right )+u \, \mathbf r'\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right ), \qquad u \in (-\infty, \infty).
$$

 

First, we find $\mathbf r\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,4{(\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}⟩=⟨0,1,{\pi }^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now,  we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{t}^{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,8t⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,8(\frac{\pi }{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,0,4\pi ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the given curve at the point $P$ where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(u)=⟨0,1,{\pi }^{2}⟩+u⟨-1,0,4\pi ⟩,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Given the curve $\mathbf r(t)=\left\langle t^2+1\,,\, 6t+3\right\rangle,$ find all of the points at which the tangent to the curve is perpendicular to the vector $\left\langle 3\,,\, 1\right\rangle.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf r(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1)\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6t+3)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t\,,\,6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $\left\langle 3\,,\, 1 \right\rangle$ and $\mathbf r'(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $\left\langle 3\,,\, 1 \right\rangle \cdot \mathbf r'(t) = 0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨3\,,\,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨3\,,\,1⟩\cdot ⟨2t\,,\,6⟩ & =0 \\ 3\cdot 2t+1\cdot 6 & =0 \\ 6t+6 & =0 \\ t & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=-1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨(-1)^{2}+1\,,\,6(-1)+3⟩=⟨2\,,\,-3⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $\left\langle 3\,,\, 1\right\rangle$ and $\mathbf r'(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(2,-3).$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Parallel to Another Vector
canonical_examples.problem: Given the curve $\mathbf r(t)=(t^2+t)\,\mathbf i+(t^2-t)\,\mathbf j,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $3\, \mathbf i+\,\mathbf j.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $\mathbf r(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\,j \\  & =(2t+1)\,i+(2t-1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $3\, \mathbf i+\,\mathbf j$ are parallel for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that $\mathbf r'(t)=c(3\, \mathbf i+\,\mathbf j).$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(2t+1)\,i+(2t-1)\,j=c(3\,i+\,j).\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $\mathbf i$ and $\mathbf j$ gives the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2t+1=3c \\ 2t-1=c\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get $c=2t-1.$ Substituting into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2t+1 & =3c \\ 2t+1 & =3(2t-1) \\ 2t+1 & =6t-3 \\ 6t-2t & =1+3 \\ 4t & =4 \\ t & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\mathbf r'$ and $3\, \mathbf i+\,\mathbf j$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =({1}^{2}+1)\,i+({1}^{2}-1)\,j=2\,i,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $3\, \mathbf i+\,\mathbf j$ are parallel at the point $(2,0).$
